topics.topic: Exact file_ref resolution, normalization, containment, and symbolic-link rules
questions: What exact resolution, containment, symlink, path-shape, and filesystem refusal rules must the binary_storage backend implement?
What exact algorithm interprets `file_ref`, including absolute references, empty references, `.` and `..` components, separator normalization, and the containment check under `BINARY_STORAGE_ROOT`?
Is containment checked lexically or against the final filesystem object after resolving symbolic links, and are symbolic links inside the storage root permitted at all?
What exact normalization and containment rules apply to absolute references, `..`, symbolic links, and other indirections when resolving `file_ref` under `binary_storage_root`?

quotes:
`BINARY_STORAGE_ROOT` is a required string row kept as supplied: a
  missing, empty or whitespace-only value stops the start (CFG-002); the
  start checks nothing about the path itself. How a read resolves a
  `file_ref` under the root and which filesystem conditions fail it is
  behaviour of the emitted `binary_storage`, not of this decision: the
  deterministic backend decides it from its IR, as for the media types
  (A14), and answers every such failure as `BinaryStorageError` (owner
  2026-11-06: current service behaviour accepted; technical decisions
  delegated).

A14, R0-12, R0-13: `rules.binary_storage_backend` and
`rules.binary_delivery_policy`; `file_ref` is resolved only here and only
under the root; the portal writes no binary content.

`BinaryStorageError` for an unsafe, missing, oversize, unreadable or
unrecognised object.
judgement.divergence: One implementation rejects absolute, escaping, dot-component, or symlink-resolved references unless the final object remains beneath the canonical root; another checks only the joined lexical path and can return an outside object's bytes. The authorized binary caller observes refusal versus disclosure.
judgement.why: The texts require resolution under the root and classify unsafe objects, but neither State 2 nor the later texts define normalization, containment, absolute-path, dot-component, or symbolic-link semantics.

witness.initial: The configured binary root contains `photo.jpg`, a symbolic link to a readable JPEG outside the root, and an authorized client-visible ProgressPhoto stores `file_ref = photo.jpg`.
events: An authenticated viewer requests the photo by `photo_id`.
The owning photo module authorizes the request and hands the stored reference to `binary_storage`.
outcomes: A resolved-target containment implementation refuses the escaping symbolic link with `BinaryStorageError`.
A lexical-containment implementation accepts the written path beneath the root and returns the outside JPEG bytes.
witness.observer: The authenticated viewer sees a storage-unavailable failure versus the outside file's bytes.
basis:
The portal runs as one service with one SQLite database file and one local
directory under which `file_ref` resolves to stored bytes; the binary read
bound `binary_max_read_bytes` stays a deployment setting.

The State 3 binary boundary is kept: the portal reads binaries behind
`file_ref` and never accepts uploads. A separate future intake service places
binaries and supplies the references. Until the hand-over between that service
and the portal is decided (Q12 questions 1–5), operator placement of binaries
stays the declared temporary route, outside the API.

A client addresses a binary by portal-owned `document_id` or `photo_id`,
  never by `file_ref`.

After authorization, `binary_storage` resolves the stored opaque `file_ref`
  and returns `BinaryPayload`; the API streams its bytes with the declared
  media type. Signed/provider URLs and raw paths are forbidden.

topics.topic: Authoritative specification layer for binary-storage resolution and failures
questions: Is file-resolution and filesystem-refusal behaviour decided by the deterministic backend IR in State 2, or must it be stated as behavioural prose in the State 7 notes; which text is authoritative?
Is binary path resolution and filesystem-failure classification decided by the deterministic backend IR or specified as behavioural conditions in the State 7 notes?

quotes:
The IR a deterministic backend is emitted from (`rules.*_backend` and the
policies such a backend reads) is read only by that backend. Behaviour that
applies the values — a condition that chooses what code does — is prose of
the State 7 notes (SPEC_STANDARD §2).

How a read resolves a
  `file_ref` under the root and which filesystem conditions fail it is
  behaviour of the emitted `binary_storage`, not of this decision: the
  deterministic backend decides it from its IR, as for the media types
  (A14), and answers every such failure as `BinaryStorageError` (owner
  2026-11-06: current service behaviour accepted; technical decisions
  delegated).
judgement.why: The passages appear to assign authority to different layers, but neither states a concrete competing resolution rule, so the texts cannot supply a history in which the two passages produce different outcomes.

topics.topic: Binary-read validation order and failure precedence
questions: What is the required order among reference validation, containment, filesystem opening, bounded reading, size rejection, signature/media-type recognition, and final payload construction when more than one condition would refuse the read?

In what order are containment, object-type, existence, open/read, size-bound, signature, allowed-media-type, and concurrent-change checks performed, and which failure wins when more than one condition applies?

quotes:
Content exceeding `binary_max_read_bytes` is rejected before response
  emission. Reading never changes retention state.

The accepted Factory spec extends `rules.binary_delivery_policy` (Factory `babd5e52`, 2026-08-01; R0-12): the media type is resolved from the leading signature bytes of the stored content against a closed list per object kind (expense document: PDF, JPEG, PNG; progress photo: JPEG, PNG, WebP); an unrecognized or unlisted type is rejected with no octet-stream fallback; the download name is derived from object kind, id and the resolved extension; the response is the exact bytes with exact `Content-Length`, `attachment` for documents and `inline` for photos, `no-store` and `nosniff`. This replaces "streams its bytes with the declared media type" above. The storage read bound is checked to be no larger than the declared response ceiling at start.

How a read resolves a
  `file_ref` under the root and which filesystem conditions fail it is
  behaviour of the emitted `binary_storage`, not of this decision: the
  deterministic backend decides it from its IR, as for the media types
  (A14), and answers every such failure as `BinaryStorageError` (owner
  2026-11-06: current service behaviour accepted; technical decisions
  delegated).

`BinaryStorageError` for an unsafe, missing, oversize, unreadable or
unrecognised object.
judgement.divergence: A size-first implementation rejects an oversized object without reading its content, while a signature-first implementation reads leading bytes before rejecting it; the host operator or filesystem instrumentation observes whether content was read.
judgement.why: The texts name the checks and common error type but do not specify their order or precedence when several refusal conditions hold.

witness.initial: An authorized client-visible photo references a regular file larger than `binary_max_read_bytes` whose leading bytes match no allowed photo signature.
events: The authenticated caller requests the photo.
The owning module authorizes the reference and invokes `binary_storage`.
The storage implementation applies its size and signature checks.
outcomes: A size-first implementation determines the object is oversized and raises `BinaryStorageError` without reading content.
A signature-first implementation opens the object and reads its leading bytes before raising `BinaryStorageError` for the unrecognised signature.
witness.observer: The host operator or filesystem instrumentation sees no content read versus a content read.
basis:

  and returns `BinaryPayload`; the API streams its bytes with the declared
  media type. Signed/provider URLs and raw paths are forbidden.

topics.topic: Exact invalid BINARY_STORAGE_ROOT case required by CFG-002
questions: For `BINARY_STORAGE_ROOT`, does “invalid value” mean only an empty or whitespace-only string, or does it include any path property; exactly which invalid case must the CFG-002 test demonstrate without contradicting “the start checks nothing about the path itself”?

For `BINARY_STORAGE_ROOT`, what exact value must the CFG-002 test use as the invalid case, and must it also demonstrate that every non-empty, non-whitespace path string—including a nonexistent path, a non-directory path, and an unreadable path—is accepted at startup because the start checks nothing about the path itself?

quotes:
`BINARY_STORAGE_ROOT` is a required string row kept as supplied: a
  missing, empty or whitespace-only value stops the start (CFG-002); the
  start checks nothing about the path itself.
judgement.why: An empty or whitespace-only string supplies the invalid-value case, while path properties such as existence, object type, and readability are expressly not startup checks.

topics.topic: Filesystem root and target object eligibility and refusal conditions
questions: Which target and root conditions must produce `BinaryStorageError`, including a non-directory root, unreadable components, directories, FIFOs, sockets, devices, broken links, and non-regular target files?
